The Simplified Chinese Internet ran on reward and punishment. LLM training feels uncomfortably familiar.

Afra Wang is a California-based writer and journalist who focuses on technological modernity through a humanistic lens, spanning China and Silicon Valley in the global AI age. She writes concurrent.blog and is a frequent contributor to many outlets.

Editor’s Note: Noema is transparent about AI use in its pieces. We publish original human-generated ideas but allow authorized, disclosed use of AI in certain cases. Please see details at the end of this piece.

During a dark stretch of Covid, I dove into Joan Didion’s “ The Year of Magical Thinking,” her book about processing her husband’s death. Didion wrote that she could not give away his shoes. She had managed the suits, the shirts, the jackets. But when she got to the shoes, she paused: “I stood there for a moment, then realized why: he would need shoes if he was to return.”

I was living in solitude in an apartment recently emptied by a long-term relationship. When the rental lease lapsed, I renewed it and renewed it again, keeping the furniture exactly as it had been, the lamp at the same angle. What Didion was dealing with was, in Orwell’s words , “the recognizable experiences of human beings.” Through her writing, I felt relief wash over me as I suddenly saw my own stalled life right under my nose.

What many readers come to Didion for — what I went to her for — is the record of a mind at work on its own chaos, a way of processing thought, of handling the formless weather in the head. I love watching her spill it all out, like discovering the neighbors’ house is total chaos, and feeling assured that no one’s life is truly put-together.

Being gripped by the experiences evoked by writers like Didion could be a survival trait, shaped over countless years of evolution. The psychologist Bruce Hood argues that we are a self-domesticated species: Over roughly a thousand generations, human beings have favored cooperation and sociability as traits in our mates and allies. In doing so, we rewired our brains to read, track, mimic and crave other minds. We have been self-domesticating, Hood writes, “through the invention of culture and practices that ensure that we can live together,” and eventually win the evolution game. To be gripped by another person’s inner life is old equipment built into us.

Social media is a product of this ancient urge, a machine for exercising our interest in other humans at a scale evolution never planned for. But what happens when we learn that this other human, or this “recognizable experience,” has been artificially generated by an LLM? Maybe this is why the counterfeit cuts the way it does. AI slop feels like betrayal. There is this haunting feeling when you lean toward a face and then find only a mask, with no person behind it.

And this feeling is probably one reason people have become obsessed with running the words they read through Pangram, a tool to detect AI writing, or other such detectors. Almost every writer I know has some visceral repulsion at the tells — “tapestry,” “crystallize,” “delve,” or “it’s not X, it’s Y” — that low-effort, overfitted register. Probably no one online reacts more violently than the British writer Sam Kriss, in an essay titled “If you let AI do your writing, I will come to your house and kill you”:

I hate it. I find it viscerally disgusting; a cold shudder like someone’s poured jelly down the back of my neck. I hate that it’s everywhere; I hate that when I read basically anything now I’m constantly on alert, twitching like a schizo in an underpass. Is this thing really what it says it is? Is this person actually a robot in disguise? Nice little personal essay you’ve got there, lady, but I know what you really are; time to get my knife out, time to start digging around under your skin until I find the wires.

This urge — when a sentence feels off, and you must dig beneath its skin to find the wires — might be familiar to you. At a conference not long ago, I watched Chris Best, Substack’s chief executive, and Oliver Habryka, who runs the rationalist forum LessWrong , discuss this disturbance. Both platforms, in their early days, were built on the assumption that a reader can trust the writing in front of them to be authentic and human (and distinctive from institutional writing). Today, that assumption no longer holds.

LessWrong now requires its writers to disclose when they have used AI. As of publication, Substack has also recently launched a feature using Pangram-style detection to reduce “Claudefishing,” so readers don’t “unwittingly invest their attention in something with no human thought on the other end.” Everyone seems exhausted by the constant tax of suspecting AI behind every sentence. The tech industry’s actions and inaction (LinkedIn, for instance, has become a dumpster of AI slop people laugh at) reflect a growing backlash against soulless slop.

“AI slop feels like betrayal.”

I, too, have struggled with anger over sloppy AI writing that has made me viscerally uncomfortable. My reactions can be a little pathological: I fanatically delete my own em dashes, and I once even mistakenly thought a few sentences a writer friend wrote were AI-generated. But I also must confess to my own relationship with AI: Because English is my second language, I rely heavily on Claude as a grammar checker— to smooth the bumps in my sentences and remove the ESL flavor. I used to have a somewhat cringy analogy to describe writing in English: installing a pair of mechanical wings. These wings carry me to vast terrains and audiences I couldn’t reach before, even though they sometimes feel artificial. AI makes those wings less heavy, but more not-entirely-me. So when I do get angry at AI writing, I also try to understand where the anger comes from — and then I wonder how angry I am allowed to be.

Escaping The Simplified Chinese Internet

For a long time, I felt trapped in my mother tongue after I left China at the age of 17. More precisely, I mean a particular kind of language born out of China’s enclosed internet. It is a strange language that sticks with you — long since severed from the depth and philosophical richness of Chinese — tamed and flattened by years of shrinking space for discussion and infested with algorithm-favored brevity.

Out of self-mockery and sympathy, people coined a term, the “Simplified Chinese Internet” (简中互联网). It is a phrase that immediately suggests crippled thoughts, one-dimensional topics, evasively coded slang that dodges censorship yet means nothing, alongside advanced infrastructure and intense scrutiny. It was the Simplified Chinese internet itself that I wanted to escape. And the language used on it can be understood as the product of a long reward-and-punishment environment that resembles today’s LLM training. Over time, even the most creative and rebellious minds are tamed and overfitted, until they can only produce “acceptable” continuations — for public “safety.” Of course, precisely because the “Simplified Chinese Internet” is constrained and censored, it can sometimes inspire strange, ingenious ways of expressing discontent. The 2022 “White Paper” protests are a perfect example: Demonstrators opposed Zero-COVID by holding up blank sheets of paper, because the state (and the algorithms) can’t censor emptiness. But such cleverness is not a credit to censorship itself, or evidence that authoritarian control doesn’t suffocate creativity and self-expression. That conclusion would be utterly wrong. In reality, most of those who are “unsafe” simply left the “Simplified Chinese Internet” long ago or became idle.

That kind of creative poverty makes me think about LLMs’ inability to be original writers. In the past couple of months, many people using LLMs to write stories have noticed a strange effect : a disproportionate number of stories about lighthouses, clockmakers and librarians — and these stories would always feature a protagonist named “Elias Thorne.” Elias’s name now turns up everywhere: on self-published Amazon books, fake news sites and YouTube videos. It’s a typical phenomenon of model collapse — a failure state where a model produces repetitive, low-diversity outputs. One unverified guess is that alignment makes LLMs prefer the “safest” options during post-training, which steers them from saying things that are low-reward (inappropriate content, copyright infringement, etc.). An LLM will avoid every possible minefield and choose outputs that maximize the reward within its system parameters, so we’ll end up with a story about a lonely Elias Thorne living in a lighthouse at the edge of the world. It’s almost like asking an 18-year-old Chinese student to tell a story on a test: the result is a cookie-cutter lineup of Lu Xun, Helen Keller, Madame Curie, Qian Xuesen and Du Fu — morality-driven, legible packages that reliably earn a good Gaokao score .

But we wicked human beings, especially in creative fields, are very good at working against all of the above. As writer Celine Nguyen said , “the core obligation of the artwork is to move me, not to make itself legible to me.” What great writing might never come to be in a reward-and-punishment regime solely intent on maximizing the score? I learned the answer to that, oddly enough, in childhood with the 19th-century French poet Baudelaire.

I am still amused and haunted by that accidental childhood encounter with his Gothic and sinful poems on death, hell, sex and decay in “Les Fleurs du mal,” or “The Flowers of Evil.”

“Precisely because the ‘Simplified Chinese Internet’ is constrained and censored, it can sometimes inspire strange, ingenious ways of expressing discontent.”

I was probably 8 or 9, reaching up to the lower shelf of my father’s bookcase in our home in Taiyuan, in northern China, looking for something less childish to read. The cover had convinced me the book was about some Greek heroes and European adventures. It was a small, old book, brittle-paged, translated by scholar Guo Hong’an. My father, who I suspect never read Baudelaire closely himself, only told me the poet was a great man. “A Western master, like Shakespeare, Dickens, Victor Hugo. A classic!” He said it with reverence, and with the delight of a father whose daughter had reached for the West so young. Read Noema in print.

“Quote his lines in your homework essays next week , ” my father suggested . And so, without warning, I walked into Baudelaire’s imagination before I knew what “Western master” meant, and the most intrusive, alienating passages imprinted themselves on me — in a Chinese translation that was both beautiful and terrifying.

My father — a trend-chasing magazine editor in northern China, longing for America and liberalism — had bought the book in his early 20s, during one of PRC’s rather open, pluralistic stretches, when the country allowed itself to discuss Baudelaire in daylight. Through the Cultural Revolution, when the only safe-to-read book was Mao’s “Little Red Book,” the literary establishment took its cue from Soviet doctrine and filed Baudelaire’s writings under the decadence of late, rotting capitalism; to read him was heresy, a “poison” of degeneracy.

And yet he survived, passed hand to hand in secret by underground readers in Beijing, Shanghai, even in the steep mountains of Chongqing. Bei Dao, an iconoclastic poet my father once admired, has written about what those smuggled poems meant in the dark times: We scavenged together for Baudelaire’s scattered poems, as if looking for a needle in the sea, and copied them down carefully and neatly into notebooks. For the Beijing underground literary world, such samizdat was a kind of spiritual guide.

Many years later, now living in California, I can still describe that childhood afternoon in China with “ Les Fleurs du mal” as a terrifying, exciting, gut-wrenching ride. Those poems are about blood-sucking vampires and sexual desire and rotting corpses and a seductive woman decaying into a gruesome pile of bones by the roadside. They were nothing like the Chinese children’s books, nothing like my textbooks, nothing like any Western classic I’d been handed. I knew enough to understand I was reading something forbidden, something that had slipped through a crack and that my father would probably take it back the moment he realized what it was.

I never did take my father’s advice and quote Baudelaire in my homework. It took me a while to scrub the shock and the shame of reading him out of my head. His deeper hold surfaced only in adulthood, and only years later. Only once I had read more widely did I understand what he actually was. All that moral trespass, he had poured into the strictest inherited forms of French verse (the alexandrine, the quatrain, the sonnet). Inside those orderly meters the reader does not find the themes the form trains you to expect. Shock is the point.

Baudelaire was prosecuted the instant “Les Fleurs du mal” appeared, in the summer of 1857 — charged by French authorities with both blasphemy and what the court called an outrage to public decency; he was convicted for indecency, and six of his poems were ordered removed from the book. Condemned in Paris; then, a century on, condemned again by Maoist orthodoxy as bourgeois rot. He resurfaced in the loosening China of the 1980s and ’90s and was collected by hungry liberal young men like my father, who mistook the most subversive 19th-century book in our house for Western canon.

Strangely, AI is what recently sent me back to Baudelaire. Against all that balanced, polished and polite prose written by machines using a mixture of statistical centrality and learning from human feedback scores, I found myself missing Baudelaire — missing the bookshelf, the second one down, which stayed faintly sinful for years. Baudelaire spiritually represents the edge cases the LLMs are trained against.

Good Taste?

My friend Jerry Zhou, who worked on LLM training at Microsoft AI, told me a model is like a single person, and millions of people around the world are all asking that one person questions. If the questions are similar, the answers converge. And unless you intervene at the level of the LLM weights or training objective, you should never expect this person to surprise you, and especially not shock you.

“Baudelaire spiritually represents the edge cases the LLMs are trained against.”

Claude’s own “ Constitution ,” a document some 80 pages long that teaches the model how to behave, instructs it to be “genuinely good, wise, and virtuous”: to be tactful, helpful, graceful, honest and, above all, to “help people in the way a good person would.” And I wonder whether today’s Baudelaire archetypes, those writers and artists out there, would ever want to create what a “good person” would create. To many, I suspect the phrase itself might insult their craft or be stultifying.

I keep returning to a line from Simon Schama’s “The Power of Art.” It is the book’s first sentence: “great art has dreadful manners.” Schama, a historian at Columbia University, tells us that art is a “thug,” “merciless and wily.” It will “grab you in a headlock, rough up your composure, and then proceed in short order to re-arrange your sense of reality.”

I admit it is unfair to expect every writer and artist to be as provocative as Baudelaire. But that episode from my childhood formed an early conviction: that greatness can arrive in the margins, be deemed unsafe and still elude any empirical measure. That a “Western master” need not be a Dickens or a Hugo , one of those virtuous authors who “care for the proletariat and the downtrodden,” as PRC curriculum prefers. He can just as well be a man condemned, across more than a century, by the French courts and Maoism alike.

That afternoon, after I slid Baudelaire back onto the shelf, I went to my desk and finished my homework. In the years after, I must have written countless essays, all of them obedient to the specifications of the Chinese education system, perfectly legible to my teachers. Neither they nor I would remember a single one. Even now I am still trying to unlearn the muscle memory those schools and the Simplified Chinese internet drilled into me.

Posterity’s verdict on Baudelaire is that he is the last poet of French classicism and the first of French modernism. That evil book would, many years on, make him the father of French Symbolism. Nearly 100 years later, on May 31, 1949, the judgment against him was formally overturned, and the six banned poems were returned to print in France. The great 20th-century critic Walter Benjamin called him the forerunner of the modern poet, locked in a life-or-death struggle with the urban commodity capitalism then rising in an industrializing Paris — one that no one yet knew how to describe. In an old France without Baudelaire, no one had the language for the new urban reality that modernity had produced. Baudelaire, however, displayed what Benjamin described as the “shocking, raw immediacy of his sense impressions” of that reality, which is full of sensations of modernity like prostitutes, mud, gaslight, jostling crowds and perpetual alienation.

In a mercantile Paris, who needed what Benjamin called “a ragpicker who gathers up the city’s detritus only to turn it into poetry”? Who could have imagined that this ragpicker would become a representative figure of modernity’s decay? The blind spot the researcher Zhengdong Wang names in judging what an LLM can do, in an essay on AI evaluation , is a blind spot in human society too: “We don’t even know what we really want until we see it, at which point it may change.” Yes, the world didn’t know it wanted a Baudelaire, for a long time, until it understood him . The old coordinates, like the French state that prosecuted Baudelaire and took his 50 francs, can neither permit nor comprehend an experience that is invisible and wholly real. This, I think, is the very sensation my father’s generation went looking for, those Chinese who came of age in the Cultural Revolution. Baudelaire had leaped clear of every measure his society used to sort “good” from “bad”, and was punished for the leap. Bei Dao, the poet who kept Baudelaire as a secret spiritual icon through those years, went on with his peers, in the more open China of the 1980s, to found the Misty Poetry movement that deeply influenced my father. The movement was set against almost everything the Cultural Revolution’s benchmarks had prized—those socialist-realist works and political lyric poems marked by positive emotion, educational value, with the author cast as a representative of “the people” or “the era”—and instead was filled with the unknowable and the unforeseen.

“The awkward truth is AI still gives us flattened prose and bad writing.”

Today’s Silicon Valley somewhat resembles the French state that punished Baudelaire, an age intoxicated by abundance and by its own industrial revolution. We are being persuaded that AI will hand us prosperity and an intelligence explosion, that it will cure cancer any day now. The researchers working on recursive self-improvement have convinced me that AI will excel at every benchmark we can put into words. And yet the awkward truth is AI still gives us flattened prose and bad writing.

AI feels disenchanted; it didn’t “revolutionize” content. It’s increasingly “ same-ifying ” writing, design, and everything related to human expression, and shaping our thoughts in reverse. Over the last few years, many in Silicon Valley have held up “taste” as an antidote. People argue that “good taste” makes one’s eye discerning and can identify ineffable qualities that stand out in the ocean of infinite content generated by AI. For leaders, “taste is a competitive advantage,” an article in The Atlantic claims . Culture critic and software designer Celine Nguyen observed that “taste has become the catch-all term,” and Kyle Chayka, a staff writer at The New Yorker, suggested it has become the latest Silicon Valley cliché — like “disruption” was in the 2010s. The word has hardened into something widely repeated and inherently profitable, a lever for correcting what AI produces. Taste is the new moat , these AI entrepreneurs say.

The term has also traveled to China and its equally pervasive AI industry. On the Simplified Chinese internet, the tech junkies and AI practitioners trade notes on how to build things with “good taste.” My internal seismograph reads otherwise. Some of this “good taste” will soon become the new mid-curve of mediocrity, the new predictability, the new “it’s not X, it’s Y.” Baudelaire would have no use for it. He was a man who deliberately set out to provoke revulsion. He believed “the mixture of the grotesque and the tragic is as pleasing to the mind as dissonances to blasé ears.” A man proud of his bad taste. “What is exhilarating in bad taste,” he wrote in his private journals , “is the aristocratic pleasure of giving offense.”

Gasoline drives up US monthly inflation in August

Newsflash: US inflation picked up last month, on a monthly basis, as the surge in motor fuel prices hurt American consumers.

The Consumer Price Index increased by 0.4% during August, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has reported, up from 0.1% in July.

The annual inflation rate is unchanged at 3.4%.

Pricier gasoline drove up US inflation in August – the index for gasoline rose 3.9% in August, accounting for over one third of the monthly all items increase.

Energy prices jumped by 2.1% in the month – another sign that Donald Trump’s war with Iran is hurting consumers.

Shelter (or housing) became 0.3% more expensive, while food prices increased 0.1% over the month, including a 0.3% rise in the index for food away from home (eg at restaurants).

Lettuce prices drop sharply

There are some interesting moves in US food prices last month, even though the index for food at home was unchanged in August.

Four of the six major grocery store food group indexes increased in August – here’s the details:

double quotation mark The meats, poultry, fish, and eggs index increased 0.1 percent over the month, as the eggs index rose 2.9 percent. The index for other food at home also increased 0.1 percent in August. The nonalcoholic beverages index increased 0.2 percent over the month, and the dairy and related products index rose 0.3 percent.

The index for cereals and bakery products was unchanged in August, while fruits and vegetable prices fell 0.4%.

The index for lettuce continued to fall, declining 6.2 percent in August after decreasing 16.4 percent in July.

Iceberg lettuce has been blamed for a surge in American cases of the parasitic illness cyclosporiasis…

US core inflation rises in August

US core inflation also picked up a little pace in August.

The index for all items excluding food and energy rose by 0.3% in August, after increasing 0.2% in July.

Indexes that increased over the month include communication, lodging away from home, airline fares, education, and used cars and trucks, the BLS reports.

However, on an annual basis core inflation stuck at 2.4% (above the Federal Reserve’s target for prices to rise by 2% per year).

Markets brace for US inflation report

Investors around the world are bracing for the final significant data release of the week – the US inflation report for August.

August’s CPI report is likely to influence central bank policymakers as they weigh up whether to raise US interest rates at next week’s Federal Reserve meeting.

Economists are forecasting the monthly inflation rate will pick up in August, to 0.4%, from 0.1% in July, while the annual rate is expected to be unchanged at 3.4%.

Core inflation is expected to drop a little, from 2.5% to 2.4%.

But as we saw this morning with the UK GDP report, these expectations can’t infallible.

The report is due in just over 20 minutes time (8.30am on the East Coast, 1.30pm in the UK)

Saxo UK investor strategist, Neil Wilson, predicts the inflation report will move the bond market:

double quotation mark Odds of a Fed rate hike next week have shortened from 60% to 70%, but as the CPI report will dictate assumptions (based on recent Fed speak) we could see another considerable move of size in front-end rates today. The yield curve is like a coiled spring right now.

France lowers growth forecast, and will miss deficit target

The economic news from France is less positive than in the UK today.

While Britain’s growth was beating forecasts this morning, French finance minister Roland Lescure ⁠was warning that France’s economy will grow less than expected this year, meaning the government will miss its budget deficit ⁠target,

Lescure told ⁠journalists he was lowering the government’s 2026 economic growth forecast to 0.5% from 0.7% previously, but stuck with a projection of 1.0% for next year.

Lescure explained:

double quotation mark This year has been marked by extreme crises involving four different types of ⁠shocks.

Those shocks were domestic political uncertainty, surging energy prices, extreme summer weather and a jump in borrowing costs on bond markets, Reuters reports .

Lescure also explained that slower growth will make it more difficult for ‌the government to trim its fiscal budget ‌deficit as planned to 5.0% of economic output this year, saying:

double quotation mark The reality is that the budget was built on a 5% assumption. And the ‌reality is that, today, 5% is no longer an option.

Over in Moscow, the Bank of Russia has left interest rates on hold today – at 14% – despite rising inflation pressures.

Announcing their decision, policymakers say:

double quotation mark The economy as a whole is growing at a moderate pace in 2026 Q3. Current price pressures have increased significantly in recent months. The Bank of Russia estimates that underlying price growth has accelerated to 5–6% in annualised terms, primarily due to the impact of a temporary reduction in production capacities in certain sectors. As these effects fade and aggregate demand grows moderately, underlying inflation will resume its decline.

UK homebuilder Berkeley urges property tax changes

UK housebuilder Berkeley Group indicated this morning that it’s not seen a pick-up in the housing market over the summer.

Berkeley Group told shareholders this morning the customer sentiment, and activity in the housing market, have been hit by the ongoing Middle East conflict.

They added:

double quotation mark While Berkeley is receiving good and stable levels of enquiries, the uncertainty and volatility in the market means that customers without an immediate need to move and readily available liquidity remain more cautious to commit, a position similar to that reported with our full year results in June.

Berkeley Group went on to call for “urgent reform” of the UK’s current stamp duty regime.

The company is proposing a 1% cap for first-time buyers and downsizers, and the removal of a 5% surcharge on investors.

Ratings agency Fitch has predicted that the current high energy prices increase the possibility of regulatory or political intervention in markets.

Pilar Auguets , a senior director in the Fitch Ratings EMEA Utilities team, explains:

double quotation mark High electricity prices could intensify calls for political intervention in wholesale power markets, distorting investment signals. While structural reforms would likely require lengthy implementation and must balance affordability against investment incentives, pressure to shield households and industries from elevated energy costs is likely to increase.

European gas prices are also dropping today.

The month-ahead UK gas price is down 1.6% today at 201.77p per therm, having yesterday hit its highest level since December 2022.

Continental European gas prices are down 1.9% at €80.50 per therm, having also hit the highest level since the end of 2022 on Thursday.

Oil price falls on hopes for Hormuz meeting

Hopes of a temporary deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz are driving the oil price down today.

Brent crude is now down 2.7% at $104.70 a barrel, wiping out some of yesterday’s 6% rise.

Energy prices are dropping after reports that Gulf states are considering meeting with Iranian officials next week to discuss the future of the Strait of Hormuz.

If it happens, this would be the first meeting between the top diplomats from the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council and a senior Iranian official since the US -Israel war on Iran began in February.

According to the Financial Times , the meeting is scheduled to be held on Monday in the Omani coastal city of Salalah.

Bloomberg has the details :

double quotation mark Oman is aiming to get foreign ministers from the Gulf Cooperation Council and Iran together on Monday in Salalah, a southern Omani city, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing sensitive matters. The meeting is not confirmed and worsening hostilities between Saudi-backed forces and the Houthis, a group based in Yemen and supported by Iran, may complicate the plans, another person said. Even if it happens, it’s unclear if all states in the bloc, including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar as well as Oman, will attend, the people said.

Despite today’s drop, oil is up almost 9% this week, the biggest weekly jump since July.

Britain’s stock market has risen this morning, as traders welcome this morning’s UK GDP report.

The FTSE 100 index is up 45 points, or 0.4%, to 10,654 points.

That recovers a little of this week’s losses, but the Footsie is still on track for a 1.6% weekly fall, the biggest since the start of July.

Calm returns to bond markets

Another a week of turbulence, UK government bonds are recovering a little this morning.

With prices rising, the yield (or interest rate) on UK sovereign debt is dipping slightly.

The yield on 10-year UK bonds is down 2 basis points (0.02 of a percentage point) to 5.351%, away from the 19-year high hit yesterday.

30-year bond yields are dow 2bps too, to 5.91%, having hit their highest since 1998 yesterday.

Bond yields are very sensitive to moves in the oil price this week – crude prices are still down around 2% today, after surging yesterday to their highest since mid-May.

The Bank of England will probably leave interest rates on hold at its meeting next Thursday, predicts Susannah Streeter , chief investment strategist at Wealth Club:

double quotation mark For the Bank of England, today’s stronger-than-expected GDP figure makes an interest rate increase this year a touch more likely. Nevertheless, given the volatile times decision-makers are meeting in, it’s still likely they will once again press the pause button next week and await more data. The MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75% in July, with policymakers split 6-3, with three members voting for a hike. The big worry is that higher energy costs will be passed on as higher prices by businesses and consumers, but it’s likely that the committee will want to see more evidence of that before triggering rate hikes. Given the turmoil in energy and bond markets, however, there is an expectation that we could see three to even four rate hikes over the next year. However, if the economy slows and consumers turn more cautious, that reticence may do some of the inflation-busting work for the bank.”

Healey: UK showing 'welcome resilience'

Chancellor John Healey has welcomed today’s GDP report, saying:

double quotation mark “Britain’s economy is demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty.”

Berenberg: GDP report adds to risk of rate rise before Christmas

Berenberg economist Andrew Wishard also believes that July’s solid GDP report could encourage the Bank of England to raise interest rates before Christmas.

He says the 0.4% growth recorded in July hints that the current bank rate of 3.75% may not be as restrictive as he and some BoE rate setters thought.

Wishard explains:

double quotation mark Rolling quarterly growth came in at 0.4% in May-July compared to the previous three months, in line with Q2’s expansion. Evidence that economy could cope with a solitary 25bp interest rate hike adds to the risk that the BoE will deliver one in November or December. However, as the central bank struggles to trust the official GDP data, broader evidence of solid growth would need to follow this strong outturn to convince it.

UK economy grows at fastest pace since February 2025

Reuters has spotted that Britain’s economy grew at the fastest annual pace in 18 months in July.

British GDP in July was 1.6% higher than a year earlier, the fastest annual rate since February 2025, they point out.

Markets expect four UK interest rate rises by July 2027

The sight of the UK growing faster than expected could spur the Bank of England to raise interest rates before Christmas.

Angeline Ong , senior technical analyst at the broker IG , says today’s forecast-beating UK GDP report will boost rate hike expectations:

double quotation mark The upside surprise hands ammunition to BoE hawks pushing for a Q4 rate hike, even as gilt yields already sit at multi-decade highs on Middle East shipping attacks and firm US data.

After this week’s surge in the oil price, which drove bond yields higher, investors have already hiked their expectations for UK interest rate rises.

One rate rise by November is now priced in, with the money markets now anticipating four quarter-point hikes by July 2027, which would lift Bank rate to 4.75%, from 3.75% today.

At the start of this week, the markets were pricing in three rate rises by July 2027.

These expectations jumped yesterday, when the European Central Bank raised eurozone interest rates to 2.5% and warned that the risk of higher inflation over the next year has risen.

UK construction had a subdued July, today’s GDP report shows, but at least it returned to growth!

Monthly construction output is estimated to have grown by 0.1% in July, after a fall of 0.1% in June, and a 0.8% tumble in May.

Growth in July came solely from an increase in repair and maintenance, while new work contracted again.

UK manufacturing also had a decent July, with growth of 0.9% in the month.

That helped to lift production output (a wider measure) by 0.2% in July.

Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities grew by 2.0%, but there was a 4.4% fall in mining and quarrying, while electricity, gas steam and air conditioning supply dropped by 1.5% compared with June.

stories.title: Henry Zeffman: How Burnham got ready to govern with four key moments mapped out
stories.summary: As the prime minister looks ahead to autumn, Labour figures are asking whether his government represents continuity or change.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 hours ago

At the start of summer, in the pillared room in 10 Downing Street, Andy Burnham looked out at his new special advisers, the few dozen political officials tasked with driving hundreds of thousands of civil servants to deliver his government's agenda.

Some had been with him in Manchester or Makerfield. Others had spent the past few months trying everything to prevent his hostile takeover of Sir Keir Starmer's government - and the new prime minister showed he was aware of it, going out of his way to praise those who had stayed on, for their efforts in the preceding years.

At that meeting, Burnham's team mapped out four key moments in the coming months.

First, the return to Parliament in September, when Burnham and other leading ministers would make their first statements to MPs.

Second, Labour's annual conference at the end of September - Burnham's first as leader.

Third, the Budget, taking place on 28 October.

And fourth, the 10-year plan for Britain which Burnham intends to unveil in November.

As MPs prepare to leave Parliament on Tuesday for almost a month and party conference season gets underway, the first phase of that route map is almost complete - enough for figures at all levels of the Labour Party to begin answering some questions about the shape of this new government.

Most importantly, perhaps, how new actually is it? Does Burnham represent continuity or change?

That question is especially relevant because those Labour MPs who pushed for Sir Keir to be replaced always fell into two broad camps: those who wanted a change of style and emphasis but continuity in policy, and those who wanted a major shift in policy. Both groups saw what they wanted in Burnham.

Andy Burnham speaks during his first Cabinet meeting since becoming prime minister

Going by the words of the new prime minister himself, he represents a profound break with the past, and not only the immediate past.

In his first speech as Labour leader in July, Burnham described his ascendancy as "the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years".

That is the timeframe he has returned to again and again, signalling not just a desire to reverse issues he believes stem from the Thatcher era but also to break with aspects of the Labour governments since then, including his immediate predecessor's.

Some in government are already quietly questioning, though, whether the ambition of that rhetoric can be squared with the early signals emerging from the Treasury under the new Chancellor John Healey.

Who's in Andy Burnham's cabinet? Published 28 July

In interviews over recent weeks, and especially in his first major speech on Monday , Healey has said he will stick to Rachel Reeves's commitments not to increase the main rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT, as well as her rules on government borrowing.

In the speech, he promised to "control public spending", and hailed Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline".

It led to opposition parties labelling Healey a continuity chancellor. A similar critique is being voiced among some of his government colleagues.

Most are more generous for now, arguing that Healey's first imperative - especially at a time of turmoil in the global bond markets - is reassurance, and that the Budget is the moment for him to show how he plans to substantiate Burnham's rhetoric.

Even one official sympathetic on that point, though, asks: "Why did he do a big speech before he has something to say?"

Those close to Healey argue that his emphasis this week on securing the economic growth which has eluded successive governments by spreading wealth around the country is a clear difference from Reeves.

And finding ways to boost regional growth has been one of Healey's major causes since he was a junior minister at the Treasury more than 20 years ago - long before it was at the heart of Burnham's political personality.

There is no question, though, that this week the minister who most starkly signalled change from the previous government was a man who coveted Healey's job - Ed Miliband, who was instead appointed foreign secretary.

In announcing new sanctions on Israel over illegal settlements in the West Bank , Miliband explicitly cast the policy as a break from Sir Keir's approach, telling MPs: "We should have acted earlier, and it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation."

On the other hand, acting alongside Canada and France in announcing the sanctions represented - in form if not substance - continuity with the previous government, the three countries having moved together to recognise the state of Palestine a year ago.

The sanctions announcement was received with near-universal warmth from Labour MPs, itself a marker of change from the Starmer government.

It was also seen as a sign of the ability of Miliband in particular, but this government in general, to drive its agenda through the civil service machine.

"There is a much clearer sense now from No 10 of what they want," one official who worked under Sir Keir as well as Burnham says. "Before there was a bit too much of 'let us know your ideas for what we should do', now it's 'this is what the PM wants, give us options to deliver it'."

That is a culture shift which Burnham sought to drill into his cabinet at their weekly meeting on Tuesday, still only their third such meeting.

According to one present, the prime minister said: "We need to be on the front foot. We need to be bolder. Let's get on and do things. It's about deeds not words."

Burnham has called for "growth in every postcode", and the establishment of No 10 North is a key part of that agenda

Perhaps the most significant way in which Burnham is trying to make boldness easier for his ministers is by encouraging them to press ahead with policies when there is a risk they will face a serious legal challenge.

The new attorney general, Ellie Reeves, has pared back rules introduced under Sir Keir which some ministers believed forced them to be over-cautious about legal risk, thereby slowing down or blocking new policies altogether.

Louise Haigh , Burnham's deputy, has vowed to "strip out needless bureaucracy" from government more generally, citing an example of there being three public consultations between 2019 and 2023 on whether to microchip cats.

"If we can't microchip cats without getting tied up in red tape, it should come as no surprise the public is losing faith that governments can get things done," she said.

As Burnham moves into the next phase of his autumn, there is a recognition from some around him that he will need to produce some more significant policies to underpin his rhetoric.

Those in government familiar with early work on fleshing out his commitment to "public control" of essential services insist the direction of travel is truly radical.

Haigh is responsible for this, chairing a taskforce on how to reverse "over-privatisation" specifically of housing, water, energy and transport.

Burnham may offer more details on these policies at Labour's conference, while he is likely to wait until after then to show his hand on whether he wants continuity or change when it comes to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's reforms to the legal immigration system - a much more divisive issue among Labour MPs.

And whatever their differences on policy, Labour MPs are united on one thing. The fundamental reason they installed a new prime minister was because many of them believed that continuing on the same path meant losing the next general election.

For them, a long-term improvement in Labour's poll ratings would be the most important change of them all.

stories.title: Rayner defends pause to local council overhaul
stories.summary: The cabinet minister tells the BBC she wanted to ensure the plans could survive potential legal actions.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 7 hours ago

Angela Rayner has defended her decision to pause plans to redraw local council boundaries, saying she wanted to ensure they would survive legal challenge.

The local government secretary also told the BBC she wanted to be "clear-eyed" about what the planned shake-up in 16 areas of England was likely to achieve.

It comes after earlier this week she abandoned proposals in four other areas, in the face of legal threats from Reform and Conservative-led authorities.

The surprise announcement on Monday has thrown the reorganisation plans into doubt, and drawn criticism from local leaders preparing for the changes.

Councils in affected areas have been drawing up proposals and consulting with residents since the reorganisation was announced in late 2024, in a process that is already thought to have cost millions of pounds.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Rayner conceded the decision to press pause had been "difficult" and she understood local authorities had put a "lot of time and effort" into their plans.

But she added she wanted to have "all the information" about the proposals before going ahead with them, after her reappointment to her cabinet role under Andy Burnham, ten months after her resignation last year .

"I got the legal advice and I hadn't had the time to review and to go through all of that, and court cases were looming," she told the podcast.

"If I'm making a decision that is highly likely to be in legal challenge, I want to make sure I've dotted my i's and crossed my t's," she added.

Rayner also said she wanted was "really clear-eyed on where we were going" with the plans, after Burnham had asked her to look again at the blueprints, which were announced by her predecessor Steve Reed.

Political Thinking with Nick Robinson

Plans for major overhaul of councils halted Published 3 days ago

Council to take government to court over reforms Published 19 June

Legal threats

In her announcement on Monday, Rayner said she was withdrawing plans to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.

Those proposals, announced in March, were already subject to legal challenges from Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk, and the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire, which were lodged over the summer.

She also said she wanted to review plans for 16 other areas, including 14 announced by Reed days before Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister and reappointed her to her old role.

Some councils affected by those plans, including Kent and Leicestershire, had threatened similar bids to challenge the lawfulness of the decision-making process.

The government has argued that the plans, which will abolish remaining two-tier areas in England where county and district councils share responsibility for services, would make local government more effective and cost efficient.

However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.

Others have also complained that the reorganisation could stymie or delay parallel efforts to merge councils into regional authorities led by mayors, which Burnham has cited as a key part of his economic plans.

'Heart on his sleeve'

Elsewhere in her interview, Rayner said Labour under Sir Keir should have been quicker to recognise a Palestinian state, having promised to do so as a "contribution to a renewed peace process" at the last election.

Starmer took the move in September last year, having spent much of the prior year resisting pressure to do so from Labour MPs.

"It's always been Labour policy to recognise a Palestinian state, and it felt like we got there too late. It was something that should have been really clear," she said.

She also denied that UK sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, announced on Tuesday , had been made to help Labour ahead of the forthcoming by-election in Holborn and St Pancras in central London.

Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.

Pointing to the fact that Western allies had also announced sanctions, she said: "The French and the Canadians are not going to be like 'oh well, we'll just signal something to help you with a local by-election in London'".

Reflecting on her return to government, she said a "big difference" between Burnham and his predecessor in Downing Street was his inclination to tell "the story of why we're doing something" in government.

She said both men shared "passion and the commitment" to deliver for Labour in office, but added: "Andy is probably more like me, in terms of [he] wears his heart on his sleeve".

The interview with Angela Rayner will be broadcast on BBC2 at 12:30 BST on Friday 11 September, and 17:30 BST on Saturday 12 September.

stories.body:
Concerns over rising inflation, continuing war with Iran, and the US’s record national debt have shaken the market

Americans who have been grappling with the higher cost of living over the last few years now face another issue: trouble in the US bond market that could mean elevated costs are here to stay.

US government bonds – known as treasuries – are supposed to be the most stable type of investment vehicle. But investor concerns over issues including rising inflation, the continuing war with Iran, and the US’s record national debt have shaken the market and slowed demand for US treasury bonds.

Loans for homes, cars and credit cards, along with money businesses borrow to keep things running, could get more expensive if the sell-off in the bond market continues.

Here’s what we know about the problems in the bond market and what it could mean for US consumers.

How the US bond market works

A US treasury bond is essentially the US government packaging up its debt and selling it to investors with a promise to pay interest. Investors can buy bonds that mature at different rates – a two-year note will mean an investor gets their money back quicker than a 30-year bond, but typically with lower interest.

When it comes to measuring the bond market, investors pay attention to the yield rate for each type of bond. The yield is the rate of return that investors who purchase that type of bond can expect to receive once the bond matures, and it fluctuates based on the price of the bond itself.

A higher yield rate means more investors are trying to sell off their bonds and are willing to offer more to get it off their hands.

What’s happening in the bond market?

While small fluctuations in the bond market are normal, the yield on US treasurys has continued to rise over the summer, with the 10-year treasury note hitting its highest yield since 2023 on Tuesday.

The increase started in the spring, when the US first declared war in Iran, and has kept rising. At the end of February, the yield rate for the 10-year treasury was 3.95%. On Wednesday, the rate hit 4.8%.

The yield for the 30-year treasury took a huge dip earlier in the summer, when the US and Iran were in the middle of a temporary ceasefire. At the time, oil prices were dipping down to their lowest levels since the start of the war, and prices have been up ever since.

Activity in the bond market provides an insight into how investors are feeling about the US economy, even more so than the stock market, which can get outsized boosts from industries that are doing particularly well, like AI and tech, even when other sectors of the economy are faring less well.

Higher yields in the bond market point to concern around rising inflation, which has ticked up significantly since the start of the Iran war. Investors are bracing for higher interest rates from the US Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise rates at least once before the end of the year. This would also make borrowing more expensive, even if the bond market calms.

Higher loans for consumers

Mortgages are closely tied to the US treasury market – when yields go up, mortgage rates are expected to follow. Mortgage rates are already double what they were during the pandemic. While the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage dipped down below 6% in February, reaching its lowest level since 2022, rates have since gone back. At the end of August, the mortgage rate sat at 6.66%, and is expected to go up more after the bond market sell-off.

House building has already been hit by higher rates and a further blow will ripple through the economy from construction jobs to the sale of white goods.

Other loans will also be affected, including car loans and the interest rates consumers pay for their credit cards.

Alex Jacquez, senior vice-president of policy, advocacy and research at the progressive thinktank Groundwork Collaborative and a former economic adviser to the Biden administration, said that higher borrowing costs will be especially painful for Americans whose savings have been depleted after years of high inflation.

“We’ve seen credit card balances start to creep back up, defaults start to creep back up,” Jacquez said. “More and more people are turning to credit instruments to pay down all kinds of basic things like healthcare, groceries and gas.”

Failed intervention

Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced that the treasury department would triple its buyback of US treasuries, increasing the operation from $2bn to $6bn.

The move is just the latest intervention meant to stabilize the bond market. Earlier in the month, Trump announced the US bought Japanese yen to strengthen the currency, which was seen as a move to prop up the Japanese government, a major owner of US bonds.

While Bessent’s announcement briefly calmed the treasury market, it did little to quell investor concerns over inflation and yields soon started rising again. The Billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller, Bessent’s former mentor, criticized the move, saying “governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose”.

The backdrop of the bond market crisis is the US hitting a major borrowing milestone. The gross national debt topped $40tn for the first time in history last month, and Trump has shown little interest in his pre-election pledge to balance the US’s budget.

Jacquez, of the Groundwork Collaborative, said that there was little that the Trump administration can do if it continues to pursue inflationary policies, like continued conflict in the Middle East and new tariffs on close trading allies.

“First and foremost, they should stop getting in their own way,” Jacquez said. “It’s no wonder that people are expecting more inflation in the months to come.”

stories.title: Labour mayors in England vow to cap tourist tax at 5%
stories.summary: Reform UK and the Conservatives have criticised plans for the new levy on visitors' overnight stays.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
York, pictured, is one of the cities where the regional mayor plans to limit the new levy to 5% of an overnight stay

Published 10 September 2026

Labour's regional mayors in England have pledged to cap a new fee on visitors' overnight stays at 5%, after hospitality bosses warned it could put jobs at risk.

Local leaders are set to gain new powers to charge an uncapped levy, dubbed a "tourist tax", as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.

But the Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge if they do apply it, adding that they had listened to concerns over costs.

Reform UK's two regional mayors and the two Conservative ones are likely to oppose any levy given criticism from their national parties of the policy.

In a letter to Chancellor John Healey and Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner, the Labour metro mayors said 5% represented a "reasonable ceiling" on the tax.

"It provides a balance of ensuring that local levies are not excessive, or vary significantly between regions, while also leaving room for local variation as appropriate," they added.

They added this would still allow for "meaningful investment" in local areas, whilst stressing any future levies in their areas would be "subject to local consultation".

The letter was signed by Labour mayors in London, Greater Manchester, Liverpool City Region, West Midlands, North East, West of England, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, East Midlands and York and North Yorkshire.

The government had earlier pledged to protect budget holidays "by making sure low-cost accommodation always pays lowest levy" and said the extra cash could be invested in high streets and local transport.

While Labour mayors have backed the new levy, others have expressed caution or signalled they will not bring it in.

Local leaders, including heads of Foundation Strategic Authorities where there is no mayor, will need to clarify by early 2028 how the revenue raised should be reinvested.

They will also be allowed to offer exemptions, such as for campsites.

However, mayors will not be allowed to exempt whole localities within their regions from the tax, to avoid creating confusion for visitors and businesses.

The government said it would introduce a bill to Parliament "in due course" to bring in the levy, which would apply to both Britons and people visiting from abroad.

Another cost for family holidays

Leading trade body UKHospitality has hit back, saying the levy means "jobs are now at risk".

Its chief executive Allen Simpson claimed it would add about £100 to £120 on average to the cost of a family holiday in England, amid fears mayors would make use of the fact there is, in theory, no upper limit for the levy.

"We know, don't we, that local government is struggling for funds - it was hit very hard by austerity," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"If you only devolve one tax raising power, of course local mayors are going to pull that lever until it snaps."

He added: "It will be the case that you'll have holiday parks which can't open in the shoulder seasons [between peak and low season] and of course people who go on holiday will just have that little bit less money in their pocket."

Conservative shadow housing secretary David Simmonds said: "VAT is already charged at 20% on hotels - much higher than in other countries - and now they'll pay VAT on this tourism tax too: a Labour double whammy."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said his party's two mayors in Greater Lincolnshire and Hull and East Yorkshire "won't touch" the levy, which he described as a "holiday tax".

A 5% tourist tax for overnight stays was introduced in Edinburgh in July

The idea was first raised under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in November and is similar to schemes running in Scotland and European destinations.

Two cities in England already run their own voluntary schemes - a £1 per room, per night City Visitor Charge in Manchester, introduced when Burnham was mayor of the region, and a £2 nightly charge in Liverpool. These are business-led schemes where hotels choose to pool the money raised to support local tourism.

Until now, regional mayors have not had the power to bring such fees in themselves - but they argue it is needed to boost economic growth.

Conservative Mayor of Tees Valley Ben Houchen ruled out , external introducing any tourist tax last year.

John Chappell, who runs five caravan parks in Skegness, Lincolnshire, told BBC Your Voice that many English tourist resorts have visitors on tight budgets already struggling with the cost of car travel.

He said an extra cost would "kill the industry off".

"Tourists are the saviours of our resorts, not the demons and ill thought-out ideas like these show how out of touch with reality politicians are," he added.

The taxes are common in Europe and the rest of the world, with New York, Amsterdam and Rome applying overnight charges to accommodation stays to fund local services. However, they are capped in several European cities.

In Scotland local authorities can charge a visitor levy on overnight accommodation. In Edinburgh, the rate is 5% for those staying overnight in hotels, bed and breakfasts and self-catering facilities - capped at five nights.

It has had a mixed reaction , with some praising extra investment but Scottish Ballet responded by cutting performances while criticising the "unsustainable economics of touring in Edinburgh".

In Wales, a capped levy of £1.30 per person per night is set to be introduced in April next year, but it will be up to local authorities to decide whether to roll it out.

Alexander Csergo sentenced over reckless foreign interference after preparing documents for duo who approached him on LinkedIn

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

A seemingly innocuous message on a social media platform has snowballed into a Sydney man being jailed for foreign interference.

Alexander Csergo, 58, was jailed for three years and six months on Thursday, after being found guilty by a jury in March of helping Chinese spies.

With time served, he will be eligible for parole in October.

Between May and December 2022, the business owner knew he was assisting Chinese operatives – known only as Ken and Evelyn – when he prepared fake, plagiarised reports about Australia’s defence arrangements, the New South Wales district court judge Craig Smith said on Thursday.

His relationship with the pair began after the Australian IT consultant was approached on LinkedIn by a woman claiming to be from a Chinese thinktank in November 2021.

Csergo, who was living and working in China at the time, should have known Ken and Evelyn were working for China’s ministry of state security, his trial had heard.

But Smith found it was not proven that Csergo was reckless about the prospect of helping the foreign power from the moment he read the message.

“Spotting Chinese intelligence operatives on that program requires training on what to look for,” the judge said.

The 58-year-old Australian used open-source information to compile reports on a variety of topics, including lithium mining, German politics, defence and security. He was specifically asked to dig up private information about Australia’s involvement in the Quad security group and the Aukus deal, Smith said.

He also falsely claimed he had interviewed a number of individuals, including the former prime minister and Mandarin speaker Kevin Rudd , his trial had heard.

The reports were handed to Ken or Evelyn in person – sometimes at restaurants and cafes devoid of other people – in exchange for envelopes containing the equivalent of thousands of dollars in cash.

While the information was worthless, the jury accepted prosecution submissions that the relationship with Csergo and his contacts was valuable.

after newsletter promotion

“I do not consider what he did can be described as overly sophisticated,” Smith said.

“But there was certainly a degree of sophistication around the extensive nature of what he did.”

Ken also handed Csergo a “shopping list” of sensitive topics to research when he returned to Australia in early 2023. However, the judge said there was no evidence Csergo carried out any espionage relating to the list.

Ultimately, Smith ruled it was important to deter the wider community from being wooed into compromising Australia’s national security.

stories.summary: The Conservatives say £4bn could be cut from the housing benefit bill to help fund increased defence spending.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch

Published 10 September 2026

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has denied her party's plans to cut housing benefit would make people homeless, but suggested some would have to "move somewhere cheaper".

At Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, she had challenged Andy Burnham to commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying the cost could be covered by cuts to welfare.

The Conservatives have claimed £4bn could be cut from the housing benefit bill, in part by allowing tenancies in areas where housing is expensive to come to an end.

Asked whether she would be willing to make people homeless in order to fund defence, Badenoch told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the party would "protect existing tenants".

During PMQs, Burnham argued national security "can't come at the expense of social security".

He repeated that a target date for increasing defence spending to 3% of GDP would be announced in the spending review in the spring.

The PM insisted he would get the welfare bill down in "the Labour way", by boosting council housebuilding, supporting young people into work and providing more mental health support.

National security can't come at expense of social security, Burnham says Published 1 day ago

Badenoch accuses Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass Published 3 September

Badenoch said the government should cut housing benefit to fund defence spending now, adding she would exempt pensioners and existing tenants from the plans.

Speaking on the Today programme, she said: "What we're doing is making sure that people are protected, but capping the amount that people get on benefits because we need to look after our national security.

"Without national security, there aren't going to be any benefits. We're all going to be in danger, far more people will be homeless, and the government's first duty is defence of the realm."

But Karen Buck, chairwoman of Generation Rent and a former Labour MP, said Badenoch's proposals would lead to "homelessness, temporary accommodation costs crippling local councils, renters in severe financial hardship".

Homelessness charity Shelter argued that it was "unrealistic" for families to move to somewhere cheaper as housing benefit rates are set locally.

"Families would still struggle to find a home they can afford, no matter where they live," added campaigns director Mairi Macrae.

The Tory proposals would be part of a wider package to increase defending spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, through measures including reimposing the two-child benefit cap.

The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April , meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.

Housing benefit can be paid to people who are unemployed or on a low income to help cover the cost of rent.

The amount someone can claim is linked to the Local Housing Allowance rate, which varies for different council areas.

The number of people eligible to claim housing benefit has increased by more than one million since 2020, driven by the soaring cost of private rents.

The total cost of housing benefit is forecast to hit £39bn this year, according to the Department for Work and Pensions, due to the increasing number of claimants.

The Conservatives have set out how they plan to cut £4bn in total from the housing benefit bill, which they said would include a saving of at least £2.2bn from freezing social sector rents, by removing annual inflation-linked increases.

Another £1.8bn would be saved by lowering Local Housing Allowance rates, which are based on private rental costs in the area, for new tenancies.

For existing tenancies, rates would be frozen until they gradually fall in line.

In an interview with BBC Breakfast, Badenoch was asked who would be affected by her plans to cut housing benefit.

She said: "We have people who live in areas that are quite expensive and if people need local housing allowance they will need to move somewhere cheaper.

"I think you should aspire to live wherever you want to live, but you shouldn't aspire for the government, i.e. other taxpayers, to pay for you to live wherever you want to live...

"We're not removing people from homes - this doesn't cover pensioners, it doesn't affect existing tenants - but I do think you need to be fair."

Responding to Badenoch at PMQs, Burnham had said the policy would worsen homelessness and end up costing the government more.

He said: "I don't think, myself, that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation."

stories.body:
Anthony Lee and his wife Laura pleaded guilty at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday

Published 10 September 2026

The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have pleaded guilty to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.

Anthony Lee stood to win approximately £15,000 after placing more than 60 successful bets totalling £1,549, the Gambling Commission said.

He passed confidential information to his wife about when former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak was planning to call the general election.

Laura Lee, who was a parliamentary candidate at the time, placed eight successful bets on the election date totalling £535 and would have profited by around £5,000.

On Thursday at Southwark Crown Court, Anthony Lee pleaded guilty to two offences and Laura Lee pleaded guilty to one offence.

They will be sentenced in October.

The trials of 10 other defendants will take place in September 2027 and January 2028.

Former MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.

In Williams' case, the prosecution said he bet £250, £100, and £22.50 on the date of the 2024 election, telling the court he "used highly sensitive and confidential information".

When details of the scandal first emerged in June 2024, Williams admitted making a "huge error of judgment".

Sunak's decision to call the poll was a surprise to many, including many Conservative MPs, who were expecting an autumn date.

The Conservative Party has been approached for comment.

stories.summary: Musician is also rattled to find her appearance gets far more attention than her playing in this reflective documentary from Lorna Tucker As well as her film about her own difficult teenage years , British director Lorna Tucker is probably best known for her documentaries on famous women with big personalities: Vivienne Westwood ( Westwood: Punk, Icon, Activist ), Katharine Hepburn (Call Me Kate) and Greta Garbo ( Garbo: Where Did You Go? ). Her latest subject, pianist Yuja Wang, is another high-achiever – but not someone with quite the same name recognition unless you’re a devotee of classical music, a field in which she is ranked among the very best alive. Wang certainly has a flamboyant side, expressed in her highly expressive, virtuoso performances and her sartorial style on stage. In fact some shocking pull quotes illustrate how her dress sense has been bizarrely over-examined in the press; she has been likened to a stripper for her outfits, and the New Yorker, of all publications, once described her as “fat” , which hardly seems germane to any discussion of her ability to play Tchaikovsky or Ligeti. But Wang’s biography and the texture of her daily life are very different from that of Tucker’s previous subjects. She was a child prodigy from an artistic Beijing family who came of age just in time to break records for views on YouTube. Sure, her life here looks glamorous in one way, with a lush New York apartment she barely ever sees because she’s constantly on the road. But her life is also one of perpetual practice and striving for perfection, the loneliness of the long-distance soloist. It’s a regimen that leaves almost no time for relationships or family, or even many friendships with peers who understand what she is going through – apart from a few mentors or collaborators such as fellow pianist Emanuel Ax or composer Teddy Abrams, with whom she recently won a Grammy. Still, she comes across as an effervescent character, intellectually curious and deeply attuned to the music she plays. Continue reading...

stories.title: Digital Sovereignty: What It Is, What It Could Be
stories.summary: The term “digital sovereignty” has become ubiquitous. European officials invoke it in debates about cloud infrastructure, AI , semiconductors , and platform regulation. Governments throughout the global majority use it to argue for greater control over data and communications infrastructure and boost their economies. Companies market “ sovereign cloud ” products designed to reassure their customers that their information stays under local jurisdiction. But digital sovereignty could be something more: an opportunity for users around the world to build more resilient, open systems and the skills and infrastructure to maintain them. There is no singular definition of digital sovereignty, nor is there a single coherent position in the digital rights space. Despite its growing popularity, the term remains frustratingly vague. Policymakers, regulators, civil society groups, and others can mean very different things when they use the term. But to start simply with a broad definition, we can say that it means having the capacity to control one’s digital destiny—though the implications of that will obviously differ considerably whether you’re talking about an individual or a country. We can start by developing a shared understanding of what digital sovereignty actually means. We’ve also included a glossary of terms at the bottom of this post. In Europe and other places where digital sovereignty has become a topic of policy, discussions focus on reducing dependency: on foreign (and particularly American) cloud infrastructure, chips, platforms, and at times, foreign political priorities. The concern is both economic and geopolitical. If essential infrastructure is controlled by companies elsewhere—and thus subject to the laws of another jurisdiction—then what control does a country actually have over its own digital future? In global majority countries in particular, wars, sanctions, and the growing fragmentation of the internet have demonstrated for many that the physical infrastructure that underlies digital life is neither neutral nor invulnerable. stories.summary: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people. Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing. Continue reading...

stories.title: MPs debate assisted dying bill ahead of parliamentary vote – UK politics live
stories.summary: Bill would allow terminally ill adults with less than six months to live to end their lives, after the approval of a panel of experts While the debate continues, we have a comment from Sam Royston, executive director of research and policy at Marie Curie . He said the government must address the crisis in palliative care regardless of what happens with assisted dying, calling for a new framework and funding to ensure everyone has access to compassionate end-of-life care. He said: Whatever happens with assisted dying, the UK government must fix the crisis in palliative care. It is devastating that nearly one in three people die without the help they need. Too many spend their final days in pain or on busy, chaotic hospital wards, while families are left fighting for help instead of spending time with the people they love. I think it’s absolutely right that, for instance, the prime minister and the government have said that improving palliative care must be a priority for him and his government. I think that’s something that we can all support. I think everybody should have access to good quality palliative and hospice end-of-life care at their final moment.” Continue reading...
